# Telemetry: A Textbook Chapter for the `telemetry` Package

> **AI assistant load scope (Claude Code, Gemini):**
>
> **Load when:** explaining, teaching, or changing `TelemetryProvider` or `ExporterType`, in Java or in
> the Python twin.
>
> **Do NOT load for:** logging (see [log/README.md](../log/README.md)), or OpenTelemetry questions that
> do not touch this package.
>
> **Authoritative scope:** a beginner-level explanation of the code. The Java source files and their
> Javadoc are the authoritative description of the behavior. Section 9 lists behavior that was
> checked against the code on 2026-10-16 and that may change when the code is fixed.

This chapter explains the package `org.cassandragargoyle.api.telemetry`. It has two files:
[`ExporterType.java`](ExporterType.java), an `enum` with three values, and
[`TelemetryProvider.java`](TelemetryProvider.java), a class that sets up **tracing** with the
library **OpenTelemetry** in one call.

You need basic Java: classes, methods, `if`, `switch`, and `try`. It helps if you have read the
chapter about [logging](../log/README.md), because tracing is its big brother.

**What you will learn:**

1. What a **trace** and a **span** are, and why a log is not enough to find a slow step
2. How the **builder pattern** makes a complicated object easy to create
3. Why the default mode is a **NoOp** object that does nothing, and why that is a good idea
4. How **environment variables** change the behavior of a program without a new build
5. How **sampling** keeps only some traces, and why the trace id decides
6. Why spans are sent in **batches**, and why you must call `shutdown()`

---

## 1. The problem: which step is slow?

You click **Buy** in an online shop. After two seconds the page says *"Thank you for your order"*.
Two seconds is too long. But which step was slow? Checking the stock? The payment? The e-mail?

A log tells you **what** happened: `INFO: payment done`. It does not tell you **how long** each
step took, and it does not tell you **which lines belong to the same order** when a hundred people
buy at the same time.

**Tracing** answers both questions. It is used by almost every big web service, by cloud platforms,
and by tools that watch programs in production, such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or Zipkin.
**OpenTelemetry** (often written OTel) is the free, open standard for it. It has libraries for Java,
Python, Go, JavaScript, and many other languages, so a trace can go through programs written in
different languages.

## 2. The basic idea: traces and spans

A **span** is one measured step: it has a name, a start time, an end time, and some extra values
called **attributes**. A **trace** is the whole story of one request: a tree of spans. The first
span is the **parent**; the steps inside it are its **children**.

![A trace drawn as a timeline: the parent span handle order takes about 180 ms and contains the child spans check stock 20 ms, pay 120 ms and send e-mail 40 ms; all four spans share one trace id](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every span gets two random numbers:

- the **trace id** (128 bits) is the same for all spans of one trace, so a tool can collect them
- the **span id** (64 bits) is different for each span

With this picture the answer is easy: `pay` takes two thirds of the time. That is the step to
make faster.

Here is how one span looks in the console output of the example program in section 12:

![A console line of the span pay split into span name, trace id with 32 hex digits, span id with 16 hex digits, and the span kind INTERNAL](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 3. Why not set up OpenTelemetry in every program?

OpenTelemetry is powerful, but the setup is long. You need a **resource** (who sends the data), a
**sampler** (which traces to keep), an **exporter** (where to send them), a **span processor** (when
to send them), a **tracer provider** that joins all of these, and an SDK object around it. That is
about 20 lines, and every line has options.

If every CassandraGargoyle program wrote these lines itself, each one would do it slightly
differently. Some would forget `shutdown()`, some would send data in development by mistake.
`TelemetryProvider` writes the 20 lines once, with good defaults, and every program needs only a few
lines to use it.

## 4. The smart idea: three modes and a builder

### Three modes

![Your code creates spans; with NONE nothing is recorded, with CONSOLE a SimpleSpanProcessor writes them to the log for development, with OTLP a BatchSpanProcessor sends them over the network for production](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[`ExporterType.java`](ExporterType.java) names the three modes:

```java
public enum ExporterType
{
	/** No-op exporter, zero overhead */
	NONE,

	/** Console/logging exporter for development */
	CONSOLE,

	/** OTLP exporter for production use */
	OTLP
}
```

An `enum` is a type with a fixed list of values. The compiler checks it, so you cannot write
`ExporterType.CONSOL` by mistake. A `String` like `"consol"` would compile and fail later.

**OTLP** is the OpenTelemetry Protocol: the standard format in which a program sends its spans over
the network to a **collector** or straight to a tool like Jaeger.

### The builder pattern

A provider has six settings. A constructor with six parameters is hard to read:
`new TelemetryProvider("shop", true, OTLP, "http://...", "grpc", 0.1)`. Which number is what?

The **builder pattern** solves this. A helper object collects the settings one by one with
readable method names, and `build()` creates the real object at the end:

```java
TelemetryProvider telemetry = TelemetryProvider.builder("online-shop")
	.exporter(ExporterType.OTLP)
	.endpoint("http://collector:4317")
	.sampleRate(0.1)
	.build();
```

Every setter returns the builder itself (`return this;`), so the calls can be chained. Settings
you do not call keep their default value. You know this pattern from `StringBuilder`, and Java uses
it in many places, for example `HttpRequest.newBuilder()`.

**Try it yourself:** Write the builder call for a provider named `school-app` that writes spans to
the console and keeps every trace. Which methods can you leave out? (Answer: `sampleRate`, because
1.0 is the default.)

## 5. From the idea to the code

| Method | What it does |
| ------ | ------------ |
| `TelemetryProvider.noOp()` | returns the shared provider that records nothing |
| `TelemetryProvider.builder(serviceName)` | starts a builder; the name must not be empty |
| `Builder.enabled`, `exporter`, `endpoint`, `protocol`, `sampleRate`, `serviceName` | set one option and return the builder |
| `Builder.build()` | creates the provider |
| `getTracer(name)` | returns a `Tracer`, the object that creates spans |
| `shutdown()` | sends the spans that wait in memory and stops the provider |
| `enableTraceLogging()` | makes the console output of OpenTelemetry visible |
| `isNoOp()` | tells if the provider records nothing |

### Step 1: the NoOp provider

```java
private static final TelemetryProvider NOOP_INSTANCE = new TelemetryProvider(
	OpenTelemetry.noop(), null, true
);

public static TelemetryProvider noOp()
{
	return NOOP_INSTANCE;
}
```

`OpenTelemetry.noop()` returns an object that has all the methods of a real OpenTelemetry, but its
methods do nothing. Your code can create spans, set attributes, and end spans, and nothing is
stored. This is the **Null Object pattern**: instead of `null`, which crashes with a
`NullPointerException`, you get an object that safely does nothing. Your code needs no
`if (telemetry != null)` checks.

There is only one NoOp provider. It is created once, in a `static final` field, and `noOp()` always
returns the same object. An object that exists only once is a **singleton**.

### Step 2: the name is required

```java
public static Builder builder(String serviceName)
{
	if (serviceName == null || serviceName.isBlank())
	{
		throw new IllegalArgumentException("Service name must not be null or blank");
	}
	return new Builder(serviceName);
}
```

The service name says **who** sent a span. Without it, the spans of ten programs would be mixed in
one tool. So the builder refuses an empty name at once, with a clear message. This is called
**fail fast**: report a mistake as early as possible, where it is easy to find.

### Step 3: build, in the right order

```java
public TelemetryProvider build()
{
	if (!enabled)
	{
		return TelemetryProvider.noOp();
	}

	// Apply environment variable overrides
	applyEnvironmentOverrides();

	if (exporter == ExporterType.NONE)
	{
		return TelemetryProvider.noOp();
	}
```

The order of these lines matters:

1. `enabled(false)` wins over everything. A program can switch tracing off for good, for example
   in a unit test
2. Then the environment variables can change the settings (step 4)
3. If the exporter is still `NONE`, the NoOp provider is returned. `NONE` is the default, so a
   program that only calls `builder("x").build()` records nothing until someone sets an exporter

After these checks, `build()` creates the real objects:

```java
Resource resource = Resource.getDefault().merge(
	Resource.create(Attributes.of(
		AttributeKey.stringKey("service.name"), serviceName
	))
);

Sampler sampler = createSampler();
SpanExporter spanExporter = createSpanExporter();

SdkTracerProvider tracerProvider = SdkTracerProvider.builder()
	.setResource(resource)
	.setSampler(sampler)
	.addSpanProcessor(createSpanProcessor(spanExporter))
	.build();
```

| In the picture of section 4 | In the code |
| --------------------------- | ----------- |
| who sends | `Resource` with the attribute `service.name` |
| which traces to keep | `createSampler()` (section 6) |
| where to send | `createSpanExporter()`: `LoggingSpanExporter` for CONSOLE, OTLP over gRPC or HTTP |
| when to send | `createSpanProcessor()`: simple for CONSOLE, batch for OTLP (section 7) |

Look at the line `.addSpanProcessor(...)` in the middle. OpenTelemetry itself uses builders too.

### Step 4: environment variables win

![Configuration layers: the defaults in the code, then the builder methods, then the OTEL environment variables, which win; enabled(false) returns NoOp before the environment is read](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

An **environment variable** is a named value that the operating system gives to every program it
starts. You set it outside the program, so you can change the behavior without a new build:

```bash
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console java -jar shop.jar
```

```java
String envExporter = System.getenv(ENV_OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER);
if (envExporter != null && !envExporter.isBlank())
{
	switch (envExporter.toLowerCase())
	{
		case "otlp":
			exporter = ExporterType.OTLP;
			break;
		case "logging":
		case "console":
			exporter = ExporterType.CONSOLE;
			break;
		case "none":
			exporter = ExporterType.NONE;
			break;
		default:
			LOG.log(Level.WARNING,
				"Unknown OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER value: {0}, using configured default",
				envExporter);
	}
}
```

| Environment variable | Changes |
| -------------------- | ------- |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | the service name |
| `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER` | `otlp`, `console` or `logging`, `none` |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | the address of the collector |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `grpc` or `http/protobuf` |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `always_on`, `always_off`, `traceidratio` |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` | the sample rate for `traceidratio` |

These names are not invented by this project. They are the **standard** names from the OpenTelemetry
specification, so an operator who knows OpenTelemetry knows them already.

> **Watch out:** an unknown value does not stop the program. `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=jaeger` logs a
> warning and keeps the value from the builder. Read the warnings in the log when tracing does not
> work as you expect.

## 6. Sampling: keep only some traces

A busy shop has thousands of orders per minute. Sending every trace costs network, storage, and
money. **Sampling** keeps only a part: with `sampleRate(0.3)` about 30 % of the traces.

```java
if (sampleRate >= 1.0)
{
	return Sampler.alwaysOn();
}
if (sampleRate <= 0.0)
{
	return Sampler.alwaysOff();
}
return Sampler.traceIdRatioBased(sampleRate);
```

How does `traceIdRatioBased` decide? It does **not** roll a dice. It reads the last 16 hex digits
of the trace id as a number, turns it into a score between 0 and 1, and keeps the trace when the
score is below the rate:

![Ten trace ids with the score of their last 16 hex digits between 0 and 1; the three with a score below 0.3 are kept, the seven others are dropped, including one with 0.303](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The trace id is random, so about 30 % of the ids have a score below 0.3. But for **one** trace
the answer is always the same. When the shop calls the payment service, both programs see the same
trace id and make the same decision, so you never get half a trace.

The builder checks the rate: `sampleRate(1.5)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. The environment
variable `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` can choose the sampler directly; it is read in `createSampler()`.

## 7. Simple or batch: when does a span leave?

![SimpleSpanProcessor exports every span at once, one by one; BatchSpanProcessor collects spans in a queue in memory and sends many in one network call, and shutdown sends the rest](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```java
private io.opentelemetry.sdk.trace.SpanProcessor createSpanProcessor(SpanExporter spanExporter)
{
	if (exporter == ExporterType.CONSOLE)
	{
		return SimpleSpanProcessor.create(spanExporter);
	}
	return BatchSpanProcessor.builder(spanExporter).build();
}
```

In development you want to see every span at once, so CONSOLE uses the **simple** processor. In
production a network call for every span would be slow, so OTLP uses the **batch** processor. It
keeps spans in a queue in memory and sends many at once from a background thread.

The price of the batch: when the program ends, some spans still wait in the queue. That is why
`shutdown()` exists:

```java
public void shutdown()
{
	if (!noOp && sdkTracerProvider != null)
	{
		LOG.log(Level.FINE, "Shutting down TelemetryProvider, flushing pending spans");
		sdkTracerProvider.forceFlush().join(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
		sdkTracerProvider.shutdown().join(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
	}
}
```

`forceFlush()` sends everything in the queue, `shutdown()` stops the background thread. Each step
waits at most 5 seconds, so a collector that does not answer cannot stop your program from ending.
Calling `shutdown()` on the NoOp provider is safe and does nothing.

> **Watch out:** forget `shutdown()` and the last spans before the end of the program are lost. Put
> it in a `finally` block or in a shutdown hook.

## 8. Showing the console output

The CONSOLE exporter writes spans through `java.util.logging` at the level `INFO`, to the logger
`io.opentelemetry.exporter.logging.LoggingSpanExporter`. If the program sets a higher level, the
spans are not visible. `enableTraceLogging()` sets the logger `io.opentelemetry` to `INFO`. It first
tries Logback through **reflection** (calling classes by their name at run time, so the project does
not need Logback to compile), and falls back to `java.util.logging`.

## 9. Traps we found in this code

We checked each of these with a small program on 2026-10-16. They may be fixed when you read this.

### Trap 1: no trace context goes to other programs

The main `README.md` of the project says "W3C TraceContext propagation". **Propagation** means that
the trace id travels with a request to the next program, in the HTTP header `traceparent`, so both
programs add spans to the same trace. The Java `build()` does not set any propagator, and the list of
propagated header fields is empty. To get it, the SDK needs one more line:

```java
OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()
	.setTracerProvider(tracerProvider)
	.setPropagators(ContextPropagators.create(W3CTraceContextPropagator.getInstance()))
	.build();
```

With it, the fields are `traceparent` and `tracestate`. The Python twin uses the global propagator of
the OpenTelemetry Python API, which is W3C TraceContext by default.

### Trap 2: the provider is not global

Libraries that use `GlobalOpenTelemetry.get()` do not see this provider; they get a NoOp tracer. Pass
the `Tracer` from `getTracer()` to your code yourself.

### Trap 3: the standard default sampler is unknown

OpenTelemetry's own default for `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` is `parentbased_always_on`. This value, and
the other `parentbased_*` values, give a warning *"Unknown OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER value"*, and the
sampler is chosen from the sample rate. And `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=traceidratio` with
`OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=5` crashes `build()` with *"ratio must be in range [0.0, 1.0]"*, because the
environment value is not checked like `sampleRate()` is.

### Trap 4: HTTP needs another address

The default endpoint `http://localhost:4317` is the port for **gRPC**. With
`protocol("http/protobuf")` the collector normally listens on port **4318**, and the Java HTTP
exporter needs the full path: `http://localhost:4318/v1/traces`. Set the endpoint yourself when you
use HTTP.

### Trap 5: small differences between Java and Python

The two modules are twins, and the project rule says they must behave the same. Java logs the line
*"TelemetryProvider initialized"* at the level `CONFIG`, Python at `INFO`, so the same logging
settings can show the line in one language and hide it in the other. `serviceName(null)` on the builder is not checked in Java, while
`builder(null)` is.

## 10. How fast is it?

| Mode | Cost per span | Memory |
| ---- | ------------- | ------ |
| NONE | almost zero: the NoOp methods return at once | none |
| CONSOLE | one log line, written at once by the thread that ends the span | none kept |
| OTLP | the span is put in a queue, a background thread sends batches | the queue |

This is why NONE is the default: a program can be full of spans and still run at full speed when
nobody needs the data. Sampling (section 6) lowers the cost of OTLP in proportion: with 0.1, about
one trace in ten is recorded and sent.

## 12. Use it: trace an online order

This program creates one trace with a parent span and three child spans:

```java
package org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo;

import io.opentelemetry.api.trace.Span;
import io.opentelemetry.api.trace.Tracer;
import io.opentelemetry.context.Scope;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.telemetry.ExporterType;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.telemetry.TelemetryProvider;

public class OnlineShop
{
	public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException
	{
		TelemetryProvider telemetry = TelemetryProvider.builder("online-shop")
			.exporter(ExporterType.CONSOLE)
			.build();
		TelemetryProvider.enableTraceLogging();
		Tracer tracer = telemetry.getTracer("org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo");

		Span order = tracer.spanBuilder("handle order").startSpan();
		try (Scope scope = order.makeCurrent())
		{
			order.setAttribute("order.items", 3);
			step(tracer, "check stock", 20);
			step(tracer, "pay", 120);
			step(tracer, "send e-mail", 40);
		}
		finally
		{
			order.end();
		}

		System.out.println("trace id: " + order.getSpanContext().getTraceId());
		telemetry.shutdown();
	}

	private static void step(Tracer tracer, String name, long millis) throws InterruptedException
	{
		Span span = tracer.spanBuilder(name).startSpan();
		try
		{
			Thread.sleep(millis);
		}
		finally
		{
			span.end();
		}
	}
}
```

`order.makeCurrent()` makes `handle order` the **current span**. Every span that starts while it is
current becomes its child, so you do not pass the parent by hand. The `try`-with-resources block
ends the "current" state, and `finally` ends the span even when a step throws an exception.

Build the project once (`make build-java`). The program needs the OpenTelemetry libraries, so let
Maven write the class path into a file, then compile and run the demo from the repository root:

```bash
mvn -q -f java/pom.xml dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=cp.txt
javac -cp java/target/classes:$(cat java/cp.txt) -d demo-out org/cassandragargoyle/api/demo/OnlineShop.java
java -cp java/target/classes:$(cat java/cp.txt):demo-out org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.OnlineShop
```

Output (your ids and times are different, because they are random and current):

```text
Oct 16, 2026 9:21:18 PM io.opentelemetry.exporter.logging.LoggingSpanExporter export
INFO: 'check stock' : 85960971ce9b618c58ff4e18169e6958 912a542020a52091 INTERNAL [tracer: org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo:] {}
Oct 16, 2026 9:21:18 PM io.opentelemetry.exporter.logging.LoggingSpanExporter export
INFO: 'pay' : 85960971ce9b618c58ff4e18169e6958 ff2c3724e13d56f8 INTERNAL [tracer: org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo:] {}
Oct 16, 2026 9:21:18 PM io.opentelemetry.exporter.logging.LoggingSpanExporter export
INFO: 'send e-mail' : 85960971ce9b618c58ff4e18169e6958 70633c79d5233d0d INTERNAL [tracer: org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo:] {}
Oct 16, 2026 9:21:18 PM io.opentelemetry.exporter.logging.LoggingSpanExporter export
INFO: 'handle order' : 85960971ce9b618c58ff4e18169e6958 d35e1bf8e169ea30 INTERNAL [tracer: org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo:] AttributesMap{data={order.items=3}, capacity=128, totalAddedValues=1}
trace id: 85960971ce9b618c58ff4e18169e6958
```

Look at the order: the children are printed **before** the parent. A span is exported when it ends,
and the parent ends last. All four lines have the same trace id.

## 13. Exercises

Try each exercise on your own first, then check your answer in section 15.

**1.** What does `TelemetryProvider.builder("app").build().isNoOp()` return when no `OTEL_`
environment variable is set? Why?

**2.** The trace id `ed038db4de38378426d0b944a2863a7f` has the score 0.303. Is it kept with
`sampleRate(0.3)`? And with `sampleRate(0.31)`?

**3.** A program calls `builder("app").enabled(false).exporter(ExporterType.CONSOLE).build()`, and
the variable `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp` is set. Is the result a NoOp provider?

**4.** What happens with `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=jaeger` and a builder without `exporter(...)`?

**5.** Why does the OTLP mode use a `BatchSpanProcessor`, and what do you lose when you forget
`shutdown()`?

**6.** In `OnlineShop`, move the line `order.end()` from `finally` to just after the line
`order.setAttribute(...)`. What changes in the trace?

**7.** *(Challenge.)* Fix trap 1: add W3C TraceContext propagation to `build()`, and write a JUnit
test that checks that the propagator of a CONSOLE provider has the fields `traceparent` and
`tracestate`. Hint: the test needs access to the `OpenTelemetry` object, so add a getter
`getOpenTelemetry()` first.

## 14. Words to remember

| Term | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| Telemetry | data that a program sends about itself while it runs: traces, metrics, logs |
| Trace | the whole story of one request, a tree of spans with one trace id |
| Span | one measured step with a name, a start, an end, and attributes |
| Attribute | a named value on a span, for example `order.items = 3` |
| Exporter | the part that sends spans somewhere: the console or the network |
| OTLP | the OpenTelemetry Protocol for sending telemetry over gRPC or HTTP |
| Sampling | keeping only a part of the traces |
| Builder pattern | an object that collects settings with named methods and creates the real object in `build()` |
| Null Object pattern | an object that safely does nothing, used instead of `null` |
| Singleton | an object that exists only once |
| Fail fast | report a wrong input at once, where the mistake is easy to find |
| Environment variable | a named value that the operating system gives to a program when it starts |
| Propagation | sending the trace id with a request to the next program |

## 15. Answers

**1.** `true`. The default exporter is `NONE`, so `build()` returns the NoOp provider. It is even the
same object as `TelemetryProvider.noOp()`.

**2.** With 0.3: no, 0.303 is not below 0.3. With 0.31: yes, 0.303 is below 0.31.

**3.** Yes. `build()` checks `enabled` first and returns NoOp before it reads the environment.

**4.** The log shows the warning *"Unknown OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER value: jaeger, using configured
default"*. The configured default is `NONE`, so the provider is NoOp.

**5.** Sending every span alone over the network would be slow. The batch processor collects spans
in memory and sends many in one call from a background thread. Without `shutdown()`, the spans that
still wait in the queue when the program ends are lost.

**6.** The parent span ends before its children start, so the timeline shows `handle order` as a very
short span, and the three steps start after its end. They are still its children, because the scope
is still current, but the picture no longer shows that the order took about 180 ms.

**7.** In `build()`, add `.setPropagators(ContextPropagators.create(W3CTraceContextPropagator.getInstance()))`
to the `OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()` chain. The test:

```java
@Test
public void testConsoleProviderPropagatesW3CTraceContext()
{
	TelemetryProvider provider = TelemetryProvider.builder("test")
		.exporter(ExporterType.CONSOLE)
		.build();
	Collection<String> fields = provider.getOpenTelemetry().getPropagators().getTextMapPropagator().fields();
	assertTrue(fields.contains("traceparent"));
	assertTrue(fields.contains("tracestate"));
	provider.shutdown();
}
```
